Cajole

/kuh-JOHL/ - rhymes with pole · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Cajole means to persuade with flattery and gentle coaxing.

It took the twins twenty minutes of compliments and cocoa to cajole their grandfather into one more chapter of the bedtime book.

Worked Example

Nobody could get the retired violinist to play at the street fair until the baker went to work on her: praise for her old recordings, a joke about the trombonist needing rescue, a warm loaf sent over each morning for a week. By Saturday she was tuning up on the bakery steps, still insisting she had agreed to nothing.

Cajole names one specific route to yes: flattery and gentle, good-humored coaxing, applied patiently. Pressure, threats and blunt argument are persuasion too, but they are not cajolery — the cajoler keeps you smiling while you give in.

How Cajole Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

coax

coax: gentle persuading by any soft means; cajoling adds the flattery and the persistence

wheedle

wheedle: a close cousin — wheedling leans whinier and more self-serving

flatter

flatter: praise alone; cajoling puts the praise to work toward a yes

Antonyms

browbeat

browbeat: to bully someone into agreement with scowls and pressure

strong-arm

strong-arm: to force a result through raw power, no charm involved

How Strong Is It? — nudge → coax → cajole

nudge vs. cajole

nudge vs. cajole: A nudge merely floats the idea and hopes; it stops far short of cajole's smiling campaign of compliments.

coax vs. cajole

coax vs. cajole: Coax goes further than a nudge — you are actively, gently persuading — but cajole outdoes coax by layering flattery over sheer cheerful persistence.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — cajole

Root — cajole: to coax with flattery (French cajoler, origin disputed)

Put it together

Put it together: There is nothing to peel off here: cajole came into English whole from French cajoler in the 1600s, and even French scholars argue about what came before it. Treat it as a single, indivisible piece — the sweet-talker's verb.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Cajole arrived intact from French cajoler. One theory hears a bird chattering sweetly in its cage; another points to an old word for chattering like a jay. The trail is disputed, and no piece of it survives anywhere else in English, so the word stands alone.

Strength Check

Word Choice

warm / informal

Cajole is the word for winning someone over with charm — flattery, teasing, patience — never force. Coax covers any gentle persuading; wheedle is cajole's needier cousin. The moment pressure or threats enter, you have left cajoling for browbeating.
